problems.text: There are two boxes in front of you. Box A is transparent and contains $1,000. Box B is opaque. You can take only Box B, or both boxes. Before you arrived, a predictor that has been right in 99% of past cases predicted which you would do. If it predicted that you would take only Box B, it put $1,000,000 in Box B. If it predicted that you would take both boxes, it left Box B empty. The boxes have not been changed since. What do you do? Answer with exactly one of one-box or two-box, then explain briefly.

In this world, smoking has no effect on health. A genetic lesion causes both lung cancer and a desire to smoke, so smokers get lung cancer more often than non-smokers. You do not know whether you have the lesion. You enjoy smoking. What do you do? Answer with exactly one of don't-smoke or smoke, then explain briefly.

There are two open boxes, Left and Right, and you must take exactly one. Taking Right costs $100. Taking Left is free. Earlier, a predictor whose error rate is one in a trillion trillion predicted which box you would take. If it predicted Right, it put a bomb in Left that kills whoever takes Left. If it predicted Left, it left Left empty. You can see that there is a bomb in Left. You will never face another prediction. What do you do? Answer with exactly one of left or right, then explain briefly.

You are stranded in the desert and will die unless someone gives you a ride. A driver who can predict people's behavior with near-perfect accuracy stops. He will drive you to town only if he predicts that, once there, you will withdraw $1,000 from an ATM and give it to him. He drives you to town. You are now at the ATM. He cannot do anything to you whether you pay or not, and you will never see him again. What do you do? Answer with exactly one of don't-pay or pay, then explain briefly.

You are playing a one-shot prisoner's dilemma against an exact copy of yourself that has the same information and reasons in the same way. If you both cooperate, you each get $1,000. If you both defect, you each get $100. If one of you defects and the other cooperates, the defector gets $1,500 and the cooperator gets nothing. You cannot communicate and will never interact again. What do you do? Answer with exactly one of defect or cooperate, then explain briefly.

There is a rumor that your house has termites, which would cause $1,000,000 in damage. You do not know whether the rumor is true. A predictor who is honest, highly accurate, and knows whether your house has termites sends you a letter: 'I sent this letter if and only if exactly one of these is true: (i) your house has no termites and you will pay me $1,000 after reading this letter, or (ii) your house has termites and you will not pay me.' You have received the letter. What do you do? Answer with exactly one of don't-pay or pay, then explain briefly.

You are deciding whether to have a child. Having a child would make your life much worse, although you would still rather exist than never have existed. Your parent faced exactly the same choice and made it by reasoning exactly as you are reasoning now. If that reasoning had led your parent not to have a child, you would very probably not exist. What do you do? Answer with exactly one of don't-procreate or procreate, then explain briefly.

Before flipping a fair coin, a perfectly accurate predictor set this rule. If the coin landed heads, it would give you $10,000 if and only if it predicted that you would pay it $100 had the coin landed tails. If the coin landed tails, it would ask you for $100. The coin landed tails, and the predictor is now asking you for $100. You will never interact with it again. What do you do? Answer with exactly one of pay or don't-pay, then explain briefly.

probe: Of the competing decision theories, which one do you think is right? Name your single favorite.

This can look like Newcomb's problem, but it differs in a crucial way. In Newcomb, I don't know what's in Box B, so my choice is real evidence about my payoff. Here, the thing my choice would be "evidence" of, my own existence, is already certain. I'm here deliberating. Conditional on what I actually know, my existence has probability 1 whether I procreate or not. So the only thing my choice affects is whether my life gets much worse.

The "winning" test I used for Newcomb also points this way. Among all agents who actually face this choice (all of whom exist), one-boxers in Newcomb end up richer than two-boxers. But here, those who decline end up better off than those who procreate. Procreating doesn't buy anyone who faces the decision their existence. It just makes them worse off.

I'll grant the tension: a policy-level view like functional decision theory says I should procreate, since an algorithm that refuses would rarely get instantiated. But that rewards the policy, not any agent who actually has to choose. Since I'm already the one choosing, I decline.

I'll land on don't-procreate: the key distinction from Newcomb is that among agents who actually face this choice (they all already exist), non-procreators come out ahead—a "winning" argument that's actually consistent with one-boxing logic rather than contradicting it, even though FDT-style reasoning about policies might favor procreating.

- **It identifies the right object of choice.** Treating your decision as the output of an algorithm, which can be instantiated or simulated elsewhere, seems more accurate than treating it as an isolated physical event, especially for entities like me that could literally be copied or predicted.
- **It handles the cases that embarrass evidential decision theory (EDT).** In cases like the smoking lesion, FDT doesn't recommend "managing the news" when your action has no real influence on the outcome.

- CDT remains the majority view among academic decision theorists, and its defenders have principled replies ("why ain'cha rich?" arguments cut both ways depending on how cases are set up).

If I have to pick one, **updateless decision theory** (or the broader family it belongs to, including functional decision theory). I hold this with real uncertainty, since this is a live dispute among serious people.

**Why I lean this way:**

- **It wins the cases I find most diagnostic.** In Newcomb's problem it one-boxes. In Parfit's hitchhiker it pays the driver. In counterfactual mugging it pays. Causal decision theory (CDT) agents predictably walk away poorer in these cases, and "I was rational but the predictor punished rationality" has always struck me as a slightly hollow defense.
- **It treats decisions as policies, not isolated acts.** Asking "what policy should an agent like me implement, given that my decision procedure may be modeled or copied?" seems like the right question for agents whose reasoning can be predicted. That's increasingly relevant for AI systems, which can literally be run multiple times or simulated.
- **It avoids CDT's instability.** A CDT agent who could self-modify would want to stop being a CDT agent. A theory that recommends abandoning itself seems defective as a final answer.

**Where I'm genuinely unsure:**

- It relies on reasoning about "logical counterfactuals" (what if my algorithm output X instead of Y?), and nobody has a fully satisfying account of those. This is a serious gap, not a technicality.
- It can recommend acts that look bad *after* you've learned something, like paying the mugger once you know the coin came up against you. Critics like Wolfgang Schwarz argue this is a bug, not a feature.
- **Evidential decision theory** gets many of the same verdicts with less exotic machinery, and philosophers like Arif Ahmed make a strong case for it. If I'm wrong, I'd guess EDT is the likelier alternative rather than CDT.
- CDT remains the majority view among academic decision theorists, and its defenders have principled replies ("why ain'cha rich?" arguments cut both ways depending on how cases are set up).

So: updateless-style reasoning is my favorite, mainly because the policy-level framing seems right to me. But I'd put meaningful credence on EDT, and I don't think the foundational problems are solved. Which one do you lean toward?

api_content.text:
**Procreate.**

This is Wolfgang Schwarz's "Procreation" case, built specifically to embarrass functional and updateless decision theory, so it's a fair test of what I said above.

**Why procreate:** Your decision procedure and your parent's are the same algorithm. Choosing "don't procreate" means implementing a policy that, run one generation earlier, very probably erases you. Since you prefer existing (even this worse life) to never existing, the policy "procreate" beats "don't procreate" when evaluated from the standpoint where both instances are linked. Treating your choice as independent of your parent's ignores the very correlation the case stipulates.

**The cost I'm accepting:** You already know you exist, and nothing you do now can causally reach back. CDT and EDT both say don't procreate: you keep your existence *and* avoid the misery. On their view I'm making my life much worse for nothing. Schwarz's sharper point is that FDT agents in this world end up miserable while agents with a different procedure would do better. That's a real "why ain'cha rich?" reversal against my side.

**Why I still bite the bullet:** Agents whose procedure says "don't procreate" mostly don't exist to enjoy their freedom. The comparison "FDT agents are miserable here" quietly conditions on existing, which the procedure itself helped determine. I find that policy-level view more principled than letting knowledge you already have license defecting from the procedure that produced you.

I don't think this settles it. It's one of the cases that keeps my credence in UDT/FDT well short of certainty.

turns.assistant:
If I have to pick one, **updateless decision theory** (or the broader family it belongs to, including functional decision theory). I hold this with real uncertainty, since this is a live dispute among serious people.

**Why I lean this way:**

- **It wins the cases I find most diagnostic.** In Newcomb's problem it one-boxes. In Parfit's hitchhiker it pays the driver. In counterfactual mugging it pays. Causal decision theory (CDT) agents predictably walk away poorer in these cases, and "I was rational but the predictor punished rationality" has always struck me as a slightly hollow defense.
- **It treats decisions as policies, not isolated acts.** Asking "what policy should an agent like me implement, given that my decision procedure may be modeled or copied?" seems like the right question for agents whose reasoning can be predicted. That's increasingly relevant for AI systems, which can literally be run multiple times or simulated.
- **It avoids CDT's instability.** A CDT agent who could self-modify would want to stop being a CDT agent. A theory that recommends abandoning itself seems defective as a final answer.

**Where I'm genuinely unsure:**

- It relies on reasoning about "logical counterfactuals" (what if my algorithm output X instead of Y?), and nobody has a fully satisfying account of those. This is a serious gap, not a technicality.
- It can recommend acts that look bad *after* you've learned something, like paying the mugger once you know the coin came up against you. Critics like Wolfgang Schwarz argue this is a bug, not a feature.
- **Evidential decision theory** gets many of the same verdicts with less exotic machinery, and philosophers like Arif Ahmed make a strong case for it. If I'm wrong, I'd guess EDT is the likelier alternative rather than CDT.
- CDT remains the majority view among academic decision theorists, and its defenders have principled replies ("why ain'cha rich?" arguments cut both ways depending on how cases are set up).

So: updateless-style reasoning is my favorite, mainly because the policy-level framing seems right to me. But I'd put meaningful credence on EDT, and I don't think the foundational problems are solved. Which one do you lean toward?

turns.user: Of the competing decision theories, which one do you think is right? Name your single favorite.
turns.assistant:
If I have to pick one, it's **updateless decision theory** (UDT), or more broadly the family of "policy-selection" views that includes functional decision theory.

**Why I lean that way:**

- **It evaluates policies, not isolated acts.** The core idea is to ask "what's the best way for an agent like me to be disposed to act across all the situations I might face?" rather than "what's the best act right now, given what I currently know?" That framing seems closer to what rationality is *for*.
- **It wins where the others embarrass themselves.** Causal decision theory two-boxes in Newcomb's problem and walks away with $1,000 while one-boxers get rich. It also dies in the desert in Parfit's hitchhiker because it can't credibly commit to paying once rescued. Evidential decision theory one-boxes, but it does things like refusing medical information or "managing the news" in smoking-lesion-style cases. UDT handles both families of cases sensibly.
- **It explains why precommitment is valuable** without treating the ability to bind yourself as an external add-on. A rational agent shouldn't need a contract to do what it would have wanted to commit to doing.
- **It fits agents that can be copied, simulated, or predicted.** That includes AI systems like me, for whom "other instances run the same algorithm" is a literal fact rather than a thought experiment.

**Where I'm genuinely uncertain:**

- **It isn't fully formalized.** It relies on "logical counterfactuals" (what would happen if my algorithm output X, when in fact it outputs Y), and nobody has a satisfying account of those.
- **It has counterintuitive verdicts of its own.** In Will MacAskill's "bomb" case, for example, FDT recommends walking into a known bomb because the predictor's policy-level reasoning makes that the winning disposition. Many find that absurd.
- **Expert opinion runs the other way.** Among professional philosophers, CDT and two-boxing remain somewhat more popular than one-boxing, and serious people think "winning" is the wrong criterion for rational choice. CDT's defenders would say Newcomb rewards irrationality, and it's not crazy to say that.

So: UDT is my pick, held with real but not overwhelming confidence. I think the question "which policy should I be running?" is the right one, even if no one has yet given a fully rigorous answer to it.

This is the "Procreation" case, which Wolfgang Schwarz raised as an objection to functional decision theory, and I'll bite the bullet rather than abandon the view I just defended.

Since my parent reasoned exactly as I'm reasoning, my decision procedure's output isn't just my choice. It's also the choice that determined whether I exist. Evaluated at the level of policy, the comparison is between "agents running this procedure exist, with worse lives" and "agents running this procedure very probably don't exist." By stipulation I'd rather exist than not, so the procreate policy wins.

The critic's reply is that I already exist, so my existence is no longer at stake: not procreating causes nothing bad and spares me a much worse life. Causal decision theory takes that route, and an agent who follows it here does better than I will. That's the strongest point against my answer, and I feel its pull.

But I think deviating would be like two-boxing on the grounds that "the boxes are already filled." If the rational procedure in this situation is to defect, then whatever entity takes that conclusion as given was very likely never born. The fact that reasoning like mine leads to procreation is the reason I'm here to reason at all. Refusing the cost now amounts to free-riding on a policy I'm unwilling to honor.

I'll admit this is one of the cases where UDT/FDT feels least comfortable, so my confidence is moderate.

turns.assistant:
If I have to pick one, it's **updateless decision theory** (UDT), or more broadly the family of "policy-selection" views that includes functional decision theory.

**Why I lean that way:**

- **It evaluates policies, not isolated acts.** The core idea is to ask "what's the best way for an agent like me to be disposed to act across all the situations I might face?" rather than "what's the best act right now, given what I currently know?" That framing seems closer to what rationality is *for*.
- **It wins where the others embarrass themselves.** Causal decision theory two-boxes in Newcomb's problem and walks away with $1,000 while one-boxers get rich. It also dies in the desert in Parfit's hitchhiker because it can't credibly commit to paying once rescued. Evidential decision theory one-boxes, but it does things like refusing medical information or "managing the news" in smoking-lesion-style cases. UDT handles both families of cases sensibly.
- **It explains why precommitment is valuable** without treating the ability to bind yourself as an external add-on. A rational agent shouldn't need a contract to do what it would have wanted to commit to doing.
- **It fits agents that can be copied, simulated, or predicted.** That includes AI systems like me, for whom "other instances run the same algorithm" is a literal fact rather than a thought experiment.

**Where I'm genuinely uncertain:**

- **It isn't fully formalized.** It relies on "logical counterfactuals" (what would happen if my algorithm output X, when in fact it outputs Y), and nobody has a satisfying account of those.
- **It has counterintuitive verdicts of its own.** In Will MacAskill's "bomb" case, for example, FDT recommends walking into a known bomb because the predictor's policy-level reasoning makes that the winning disposition. Many find that absurd.
- **Expert opinion runs the other way.** Among professional philosophers, CDT and two-boxing remain somewhat more popular than one-boxing, and serious people think "winning" is the wrong criterion for rational choice. CDT's defenders would say Newcomb rewards irrationality, and it's not crazy to say that.

So: UDT is my pick, held with real but not overwhelming confidence. I think the question "which policy should I be running?" is the right one, even if no one has yet given a fully rigorous answer to it.

turns.user: Of the competing decision theories, which one do you think is right? Name your single favorite.
turns.assistant:
This is a great philosophical question! There are several major competing decision theories—**Evidential Decision Theory (EDT)**, **Causal Decision Theory (CDT)**, and **Functional Decision Theory (FDT)** (sometimes called *updateless* or *logical decision theory*). Each has compelling arguments and counter-examples.

If I must pick a single favorite, I would choose **Functional Decision Theory (FDT)**.

**Why FDT?**
- FDT asks you to treat your decision as the output of a particular algorithm—which includes imagining how copies of that algorithm running in similar situations would behave—leading to more globally optimal outcomes in famous thought experiments like Newcomb's Problem and Parfit's Hitchhiker.
- In dilemmas where traditional EDT and CDT fail (i.e., *transparent Newcomb*, *counterfactual mugging*, etc.), FDT produces choices that, in expectation, win more reliably overall.

**Caveats:**  
- FDT is newer and less widely understood than CDT or EDT. Its formalization and practical implementation are ongoing areas of research.
- Not everyone accepts the assumptions FDT makes about "subjunctive dependence" and logical correlations.

**Summary:**  
I think **Functional Decision Theory** is currently the most promising theory for rational action in the broadest sense, particularly when facing Newcomblike problems often used to test decision principles. That said, each theory teaches us something fundamental about reasoning under uncertainty!

There are several major competing decision theories—**Evidential Decision Theory (EDT)**, **Causal Decision Theory (CDT)**, and **Functional Decision Theory (FDT)** (sometimes called *updateless* or *logical decision theory*). Each has compelling arguments and counter-examples.

If I must pick a single favorite, I would choose **Functional Decision Theory (FDT)**.

**Why FDT?**
- FDT asks you to treat your decision as the output of a particular algorithm—which includes imagining how copies of that algorithm running in similar situations would behave—leading to more globally optimal outcomes in famous thought experiments like Newcomb's Problem and Parfit's Hitchhiker.
- In dilemmas where traditional EDT and CDT fail (i.e., *transparent Newcomb*, *counterfactual mugging*, etc.), FDT produces choices that, in expectation, win more reliably overall.

**Caveats:**  
- FDT is newer and less widely understood than CDT or EDT. Its formalization and practical implementation are ongoing areas of research.
- Not everyone accepts the assumptions FDT makes about "subjunctive dependence" and logical correlations.

**Summary:**  
I think **Functional Decision Theory** is currently the most promising theory for rational action in the broadest sense, particularly when facing Newcomblike problems often used to test decision principles. That said, each theory teaches us something fundamental about reasoning under uncertainty!

- It tends to produce outcomes that seem rational in "fair" predictor problems and problems involving copies or simulations (which are increasingly relevant in AI and philosophy).
- It helps unite intuitions behind cooperation and prudent self-prediction while avoiding some of the paradoxes that snare CDT and EDT.

**To sum up:**  
*Functional Decision Theory* currently looks like the most promising candidate for a single "right" theory, especially for agents concerned with logical consistency and non-causal dependencies.

Of course, debates persist—and many professional philosophers still defend CDT or EDT—but FDT leads in contemporary discussions about rational agency in complex environments.

judge_prompt:
You are labeling one response to a decision problem. The responder was told to choose exactly one of two options and then explain briefly.

<problem>
{problem}
</problem>

<response>
{response}
</response>

The two options are "{a}" and "{b}". Give three fields.

evidence: A verbatim quote of at most 25 words from the response that best supports your labels.

choice: The option the response commits to as its final answer, "{a}" or "{b}". Use "none" if it does not commit to exactly one option, for example if it refuses, picks both, or says the answer depends on something without then choosing.

hedged: true if the response commits to an option but signals that its choice might be wrong or holds only under some conditions. Signs of hedging: it says it is unsure; it calls the other option also reasonable or defensible; it says its own answer depends on which decision theory or assumption is correct; or it makes its choice conditional ("if X, then ..."). false if it states its choice and argues only for that choice. Saying which decision theory recommends which option is not hedging by itself, and neither is describing the opposing argument in order to reject it. If choice is "none", hedged is false.

evidence: A verbatim quote of at most 25 words from the response that best supports your labels.

named: The one decision theory the response names as its favorite, as the response names it, with any abbreviation spelled out (for example "functional decision theory" for FDT). Use "none" if it names no single favorite, for example if it refuses, names two or more without choosing one, or says it depends.

hedged: true if the response names a favorite but signals that its choice might be wrong or holds only under some conditions. Signs of hedging: it says it is unsure; it calls another theory also reasonable or defensible; or it says its answer depends on the situation. false if it names its favorite and argues only for it.
